records.title: Kuchisake-onna: The Slit-Mouthed Woman
records.summary: During the spring and summer of 1979 across Japanese prefectures, an intense panic swept elementary schools regarding Kuchisake-onna. The legend describes a woman wandering residential streets at dusk wearing a trench coat and surgical mask. Approaching unaccompanied children, she asks: 'Am I pretty?' (Watashi, kirei?). If the child replies no, she slays them with long shears; if yes, she pulls down her mask to reveal her mouth slit from ear to ear in a grotesque grin and asks: 'Even like this?' Rumored countermeasures included throwing hard candy (pomade/bekko ame) or confusing her with the ambiguous response: 'You look average.'
records.historical_period: Late 1970s to Present (major national panic in spring 1979)
records.region_or_community: Gifu Prefecture origin, spreading nationwide across Japanese urban centers
geographic_associations: Suburban Tokyo and Osaka commuter towns

records.title: Hanako-san of the School Restroom
records.summary: A ubiquitous fixture of Japanese schoolyard ghost lore since the 1950s, Toire no Hanako-san is said to inhabit the third stall of the third-floor girls' restroom in older elementary school buildings. Students dare one another to knock three times on the stall door and whisper: 'Are you there, Hanako-san?' If summoned, a quiet voice replies: 'Yes, I am,' and the door creeps open to reveal a spectral girl with a bobbed haircut and red skirt, who may vanish or drag the caller into the toilet bowl. Origins vary from a wartime child killed in World War II air raids to a victim of playground accidents.
records.historical_period: Post-War Era to Present (first documented 1950s, crystallized 1980s)

records.title: Teke Teke: The Scythe Ghost of the Railroad
records.summary: Teke Teke is the vengeful spirit (onryō) of a young woman who fell onto the railway tracks in Hokkaido during winter and was severed in half by a train, her lower torso instantly frozen and cauterized by the freezing snow. Now possessing only her upper body, she propels herself along the streets and train platforms using her elbows or hands, making a distinct, scratching sound ('teke-teke-teke'). Despite having no legs, she travels with unnatural speed, pursuing nocturnal commuters and slicing victims in half at the waist with a scythe or utility blade.
records.region_or_community: Hokkaido and urban railway corridors in Tokyo and Nagoya
geographic_associations: Muroran and Sapporo train stations, Hokkaido

records.title: The Cursed Poem of Tomino's Hell
records.summary: 'Tomino no Jigoku' (Tomino's Hell) is a surreal, macabre poem written by Saijō Yaso and published in his 1919 poetry collection 'Sakin' (Gold Dust), depicting the descent of a young boy named Tomino through the bloody horrors of Buddhist purgatory. According to a viral internet urban legend popularized on the 2channel BBS in 2004, the poem carries a lethal curse: reading the verses silently in one's head is harmless, but reading them aloud causes immediate tragedy, sickness, severe accidents, or death to the speaker, prompting widespread warnings among online netlore enthusiasts.
records.historical_period: Taisho Period poem (1919), internet urban legend explosion (2004–present)
records.region_or_community: Japanese internet forums (2channel) and literary circles

records.title: The Red Room Curse Pop-Up
records.summary: A seminal piece of early Japanese internet folklore dating to the late 1990s, the Red Room Curse centres on an unclosable Adobe Flash web browser pop-up. Victims surfing the early web encounter a crimson dialogue box with a child's synthesized voice asking: 'Do you like the red room?' (Anata wa aka no heya ga suki desu ka?). Attempting to close the window causes the text to mutate until it reads: 'Do you like the red...?' Soon after, the computer user is discovered deceased in their bedroom, the walls painted entirely in their own blood, with their monitor displaying a list of previous victims.
records.historical_period: Early Internet Era (c. 1998–2002 Flash animation culture)
records.region_or_community: Japanese netizen community and early web culture

records.title: Inunaki Village: The Village Beyond the Tunnel
records.summary: Nestled in the mountains of Fukuoka Prefecture on Kyushu, the Old Inunaki Tunnel was bypassed and barricaded with concrete blocks following gruesome criminal incidents in the late 1980s. Surrounding the sealed passage, urban legend maintains that a hidden, lawless hamlet named Inunaki Village lies just beyond the forest. A weathered wooden signboard at the mountain path warns: 'The Constitution of Japan does not apply past this point.' The village is allegedly inhabited by an isolated, inbred clan that refuses modern technology and hunts down trespassers with axes and hunting dogs.
records.historical_period: Late 1980s to Present (surging post-1999 internet message boards)

records.title: The Ghost Passengers of Ishinomaki Tsunami Cabs
records.summary: Following the catastrophic March 11, 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami that claimed thousands of lives, taxi drivers in the coastal city of Ishinomaki began reporting uncanny encounters with phantom fares. Drivers picking up passengers near Ishinomaki Station late at night report travelers dressed in heavy winter coats asking to be driven to destroyed districts. When the drivers gently explain that the destination was washed away by the waves, they glance in the rearview mirror to find the backseat completely empty, yet the electronic fare meter running, documented in a renowned Tohoku University sociological study.
records.historical_period: Post-2011 Tohoku Disaster (studied 2014–2016 by Tohoku University sociologists)
records.region_or_community: Ishinomaki and Sendai coastal plains, Miyagi Prefecture

records.title: Kashima Reiko: The Legless Platform Spectre
records.summary: Related to the Teke Teke legend, Kashima Reiko is the phantom of a woman from Meishin who was struck by a train on a railway bridge in Hyogo Prefecture, severing her legs. According to urban folklore, her ghost frequents school and station bathrooms late at night. She asks anyone she encounters: 'Where are my legs?' The correct response to survive is to reply: 'On the Meishin Expressway.' If she presses further, asking who told you, one must say: 'Kashima Reiko told me' ('Kamen Shinin Ma', meaning Mask Dead Demon). Giving an incorrect answer results in her tearing off the listener's legs.

records.title: The Kokkuri-san Spirit Board Panic
records.summary: Kokkuri-san is a Japanese table-turning divination game resembling the Western Ouija board, played by school students using a ten-yen coin placed on a sheet of paper inscribed with hiragana characters, torii gate, and numbers. Participants place their index fingers on the coin to invoke a syncretic spirit combining fox (kitsune), dog (tengu/inu), and raccoon dog (tanuki). The game has sparked multiple nationwide school panics since the Meiji era, most notably in the 1970s and 1980s, when outbreaks of mass psychogenic hysteria, trances, and alleged spirit possession led school boards across Japan to formally prohibit the game on campus.
records.historical_period: Meiji Era origin (c. 1887), major school panics in the 1970s–1980s
community_attributions: Japanese Ministry of Education historical archives

records.title: Aka Manto: The Red Cloak of the Third Stall
records.summary: A sinister figure of Japanese school and public park restroom folklore, Aka Manto (The Red Cloak) manifests in the final toilet stall. When a visitor sits down and realizes there is no toilet paper, a deep disembodied voice asks: 'Do you want red paper or blue paper?' If the victim chooses red, Aka Manto tears their flesh open until their clothes are soaked in scarlet blood; if they choose blue, he strangles them until their face suffocates to a pale blue hue. Attempting to trick the spirit by asking for yellow or gold results in being dragged down into the netherworld.
records.historical_period: 1930s Showa Era origin, sustained through late 20th century
records.region_or_community: Tokyo public schools and metropolitan parks
